newsitem.title: HONG KONG: DRIZZLE AND MIST MARK LAST "BRITISH" RUGBY SEVENS.
newsitem.headline: DRIZZLE AND MIST MARK LAST "BRITISH" RUGBY SEVENS.

text.p: Diehard rugby fans, many bleary of face and red of eye, refused to let typically British weather ruin the final day on Sunday of the Rugby World Cup Sevens, the last "British" seven-a-side contest in Hong Kong.

Thousands of Hong Kong residents, swelled by an influx of visitors, had snapped up the 40,000 tickets for the three days of sport -- and were enjoying the uninhibited festivities that are the traditional accompaniment to the annual tournament.

By Sunday, the all-night partying had taken a toll on all but the teetotal, the under-age or the serious rugby fans, and many revellers were still sleeping it off when the first game of the day kicked off under grey storm clouds.
Bars and night clubs in the Wanchai entertainment district -- now shaking off its Suzy Wong red light image -- have enjoyed bumper business from both local fans and visitors.
Beer hawkers found few takers early in the day for their giant jugs of brew, but it did not take long for fans to find their second wind and for consumption to soar.

Despite being crowned as a World Cup event in 1997 -- Hong Kong's last Sevens before the British colony is handed over to China at midnight on June 30 in just 100 days -- the atmosphere reflected the carnival air that has turned the annual Hong Kong event into an icon of hedonism.
Stubbly-chinned "nuns" and Elvis Presley look-alikes strutted their stuff on the terraces.
Painted faces, fancy costume and even fancier hats stood out in the often partisan but generally good natured crowd.
Many put patriotism aside to cheer for Fiji -- which has become a favourite Sevens team in Hong Kong.
The "Pieman", a regular visitor from London, known for his vast appetite for pies and beer, put in his traditional appearance displaying his trademark belly for all to see.
A host of would-be pretenders to the Pieman's title paraded their paunches in competition.

Rugby fans are relieved to see signs that Hong Kong's new rulers will seek to stamp their identity on the tournament, which represents a cash bonanza for the local rugby union and for the territory's tourism industry.
China's People's Liberation Army has formed a Rugby squad and played in a 10-a-side tournament last week, defeating the British army team.
Hong Kong's leader-in-waiting, shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, an American football fan, put in an appearance on Saturday to throw his weight behind the event.
"I like sport, and I'll continue to support sports development in the future," said Tung, adding that he was confident the Hong Kong Sevens had a long and glittering future as a Hong Kong event.
Departing British Governor Chris Patten, a keen rugby fan, said the event was special.
"I think it is true to say that there is a particular resonance and flavour because of it being the last Sevens event before the handover," Patten said.
Outside the tournament, entrepreneurs were busy cashing in on the historic event.
John Resnick, an American based in Hong Kong, hawked "the great Chinese takeaway" T-shirts, depicting a pair of chopsticks plucking up the territory.
Sarah Bullock, 16, of Hong Kong's Island School, was selling HK$150 ($19) reversible hats. One side featured the British flag, the other, the Chinese flag.
Proceeds from the hat sales go to an orphanage in Kathmandu in Nepal, and towards building a school in Nepal, Bullock said.
